items.prompt: Why does unbroken skin stop most microbes from getting into your body?

options.label: It releases a gas that pushes microbes away
options.feedback: Skin releases no such gas. What keeps microbes out is the solid layer itself, not anything drifting off it.

options.label: It forms a tightly packed physical layer they cannot cross
options.feedback: Correct — the cells are packed so closely that there is no gap for a microbe to pass through.

options.label: It is too dry for any microbe to live on
options.feedback: Plenty of microbes live happily on dry skin; dryness does not keep them off the surface.

options.label: It changes colour whenever a microbe lands on it
options.feedback: Skin gives no visible sign at all when a microbe simply lands on its surface.

items.ok_line: A wall, not a warning sign.
items.ko_line: Think about the structure of skin itself, not something it gives off.
items.exp_text: The outer layer of skin is made of dead, flattened cells stacked tightly on top of one another and glued together, forming a barrier with no gaps large enough for a microbe to slip through. As the deeper cells die and flatten in turn, they keep replacing the ones worn away at the surface, so the wall never thins out. A microbe landing on unbroken skin can sit there but has nowhere to get in.

items.prompt: Why does a cut in the skin make you far more likely to catch an infection than a scrape that leaves the skin unbroken?

options.label: A cut attracts more microbes from the air than a scrape does
options.feedback: Microbes settle on skin whether it is cut or not; what changes is whether they can get past the surface, not how many arrive.

options.label: A cut makes the skin around it warmer
options.feedback: Warmth may follow later as part of healing, but it is not why a fresh cut lets infection in.

options.label: A cut washes away the skin's natural oils
options.feedback: Losing oils could dry the skin slightly, but that has little to do with why an open wound is a route inside.

options.label: A cut opens a gap through the barrier that normally keeps microbes out
options.feedback: Correct — the wall is breached, so microbes have direct access to tissue underneath.

items.ok_line: A hole in the wall, not a change to the surface.
items.ko_line: Think about what a cut does to skin that a scrape does not.
items.exp_text: Unbroken skin keeps microbes on the outside because its tightly packed cells leave nothing for them to pass through. A cut tears through that layer down to the tissue beneath, opening a gap where microbes sitting on the surface, or carried in on whatever caused the cut, can reach cells that are never normally exposed. A scrape roughs up the very top of the skin without opening that gap, so the barrier underneath stays intact.

items.prompt: What do white blood cells do when they find a microbe that has gotten past the skin?

options.label: They surround it and swallow it whole
options.feedback: Correct — engulfing and breaking it down is exactly how many white blood cells destroy an invader.

options.label: They carry it back out through the skin
options.feedback: White blood cells destroy microbes where they find them rather than escorting them back out the way they came.

options.label: They turn into the same kind of microbe
options.feedback: A white blood cell never becomes the invader; it stays a cell of the body and works to destroy what it meets.

options.label: They warn nearby skin cells to grow faster
options.feedback: Faster skin growth belongs to healing a wound, not to how a white blood cell deals with a microbe it has caught.

items.ko_line: Think about what physically happens to the microbe once the cell reaches it.
items.exp_text: Certain white blood cells patrol the body and, on meeting a microbe, flow their own outer membrane around it until it is completely enclosed inside a pocket within the cell. That pocket then fuses with another part of the cell filled with harsh chemicals that break the microbe apart from the inside. What is left afterwards is no longer a threat, just fragments the cell can dispose of.

items.prompt: Why does swallowing your own saliva help protect you from some of the microbes it carries?

options.label: Saliva pushes microbes straight into the bloodstream where they die
options.feedback: Swallowed saliva goes into the digestive tract, not directly into the blood, and nothing there is designed to kill on contact that way.

options.label: Saliva is too thick for microbes to move through
options.feedback: Thickness might slow a microbe down briefly, but it is not what stops it from surviving.

options.label: Saliva contains substances that break down the walls of many microbes
options.feedback: Correct — those substances damage microbes before they can do any harm.

options.label: Saliva is too cold for microbes to survive in
options.feedback: Saliva sits at the same warm temperature as the rest of the mouth, which suits many microbes rather than harming them.

items.ok_line: A chemical defence riding along with every swallow.
items.ko_line: Think about what saliva contains, not its temperature or thickness.
items.exp_title: A chemical guard in every drop
items.exp_text: Saliva carries an enzyme that attacks a tough material found in the outer wall of many bacteria, cutting through it the way scissors cut through fabric. Once that wall is breached, water rushes into the microbe faster than it can cope with, and it swells and bursts. The saliva you swallow all day keeps delivering that same enzyme to whatever microbes happen to be riding along with it.

items.prompt: Why do tears help protect your eyes from infection?

options.label: They contain a substance that breaks down bacteria and rinse the eye's surface
options.feedback: Correct — tears combine a chemical defence with a physical flushing action.

options.label: They coat the eye in a layer of oil that microbes cannot cross
options.feedback: Oil does help keep the tear film from evaporating too fast, but it is not the part of tears that destroys microbes.

options.label: They freeze microbes on contact
options.feedback: Tears sit at body temperature; nothing about them is cold enough to freeze anything.

options.label: They change the colour of the eye to warn off microbes
options.feedback: Microbes have no way of sensing colour, and tears cause no colour change to the eye at all.

items.ok_line: A wash and a weapon in one blink.
items.ko_line: Think about what tears actually contain and where they go.
items.exp_text: Every blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the eye, physically carrying away dust and microbes that have landed on its surface and sweeping them toward the corner where they drain away. Tears also carry the same wall-breaking enzyme found in saliva, so any microbe that lingers instead of being washed off is attacked chemically as well. The eye stays clear because it is being rinsed and defended at the same time, blink after blink.

items.prompt: Why does the sticky mucus lining your nose and airways help stop infections?

options.label: It warms the air enough to kill anything breathed in
options.feedback: Mucus does help warm the air slightly, but that warming is nowhere near enough to kill a microbe.

options.label: It blocks all air from entering the airway
options.feedback: Air still has to pass through to reach the lungs; mucus lines the passage rather than sealing it shut.

options.label: It changes microbes into harmless dust
options.feedback: Mucus does not transform a microbe into anything else; it simply catches it before it travels any further.

options.label: It traps microbes and dust before they can reach the lungs
options.feedback: Correct — the mucus catches particles the way flypaper catches insects.

items.ok_line: A sticky net across the path to the lungs.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to a microbe once it lands on something sticky.
items.exp_title: A sticky trap lining the airway
items.exp_text: Breathed-in air carries dust and microbes along with it, and the moist, sticky mucus coating the nose and airway catches many of them the moment they touch it, the way a spider's web catches whatever flies into it. Tiny hair-like structures lining the airway then sweep that mucus, along with whatever it has trapped, steadily upward toward the throat to be swallowed or coughed out. Very little of what settles on that lining ever reaches the delicate tissue of the lungs beyond it.

items.prompt: Why does the strong acid in your stomach help protect you from illness caused by food?

options.label: It makes food digest so fast that microbes have no time to act
options.feedback: Food actually spends a good while in the stomach; speed is not what protects you here.

options.label: It destroys many of the microbes swallowed along with food
options.feedback: Correct — the acid breaks down microbes just as it helps break down food.

options.label: It coats microbes in a layer that carries them straight out
options.feedback: Stomach acid does not coat and remove microbes; it damages them directly.

options.label: It changes the taste of food so microbes cannot recognise it
options.feedback: Microbes have no sense of taste at all, so changing flavour would do nothing to them.

items.ok_line: The same acid that breaks down food breaks down microbes too.
items.ko_line: Think about what strong acid does to a living cell.
items.exp_title: Too harsh for most microbes to survive
items.exp_text: The stomach's lining releases a strong acid to help break food apart, and that same acid is far outside the narrow range most microbes need to survive: it damages the outer covering of their cells and interferes with the chemical processes that keep them alive. Many of the microbes swallowed along with a meal are destroyed during the time food spends being churned in that acid. The stomach's own lining survives because it is protected by a thick layer of mucus the acid cannot easily reach.

items.prompt: Why does a swollen lymph node in your neck sometimes appear while you are fighting off an infection?

options.label: It fills with microbes trying to hide from the immune system
options.feedback: Microbes carried there are what the defensive cells inside are working to destroy, not a hiding place for them.

options.label: It swells to physically block the infection from spreading further
options.feedback: The swelling is a side effect of cells gathering and multiplying, not a barrier built on purpose to block anything.

options.label: Defensive cells are gathering and multiplying there to fight the infection
options.feedback: Correct — the swelling comes from the build-up of cells working inside it.

options.label: It fills with extra blood to warm the area
options.feedback: The swelling is mostly extra fluid and cells rather than a rush of warming blood.

items.ok_line: A crowded meeting place, not a wall.
items.ko_line: Think about what is happening inside the node, not what it is trying to stop.
items.exp_title: A gathering point for the fight
items.exp_text: Fluid draining from tissue all over the body passes through lymph nodes on its way back toward the blood, carrying along any microbes picked up on the way. Defensive cells stationed inside each node catch those microbes and begin multiplying rapidly to deal with them, and that sudden crowd of cells is what makes the node swell and feel tender. Once the infection is brought under control, the crowd thins out and the node returns to its usual size.

items.prompt: Why does a small amount of a microbe you have already recovered from usually fail to make you sick a second time?

options.label: Certain defensive cells kept a memory of it from the first infection
options.feedback: Correct — that stored memory lets the body respond far faster the second time.

options.label: The microbe changes into a harmless form after one infection
options.feedback: The microbe itself does not change; what has changed is how quickly your own body can recognise and respond to it.

options.label: Your skin becomes thicker after the first infection
options.feedback: Skin thickness plays no part here — this kind of protection comes from cells inside the body, not from the skin surface.

options.label: Your body stops being able to catch that microbe at all
options.feedback: The body can still be infected again; it simply responds so quickly that the microbe rarely gets a chance to multiply enough to cause illness.

items.ok_line: A memory kept by cells that met the microbe before.
items.ko_line: Ask what the body itself has kept from the first encounter.
items.exp_text: During a first infection, some of the defensive cells that learn to recognise a particular microbe do not disappear once the illness passes; a portion of them linger in the body for a long time as memory cells. If the same microbe returns, those memory cells recognise it immediately and multiply far faster than defensive cells could the first time, before the microbe has a chance to spread and cause symptoms. The second meeting looks like nothing happened at all, because the body had already learned what to do.

items.prompt: Why does the area around a splinter often turn red and slightly warm soon after it goes in?

options.label: The splinter releases heat as it breaks down
options.feedback: A splinter is inert wood and produces no heat of its own; the warmth comes from the body's own response around it.

options.label: The skin thickens immediately around the splinter
options.feedback: Thickening happens later, during healing, not in the first rush of redness and warmth.

options.label: Nerve endings burn the surrounding tissue slightly
options.feedback: Nerves send signals rather than producing heat; they are not what warms the skin around a splinter.

options.label: More blood is flowing into the area, carrying defensive cells
options.feedback: Correct — the extra blood flow is what brings the redness and the warmth.

items.ok_line: Redness and warmth are blood arriving, not damage spreading.
items.ko_line: Think about what carries warmth through the body in the first place.
items.exp_text: Cells damaged by the splinter release chemical signals that make nearby blood vessels widen, letting far more blood flow into that small patch of skin than usual. Blood is warm and full of colour, so the widened vessels carrying it make the area look red and feel slightly warmer to the touch. That extra flow also delivers white blood cells to the site faster, which is exactly what the widening was for.
